prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade shape labour demand, wages and the regional distribution of employment

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. I moved to it from B018, my opening first place, on attribution and maturity grounds, and nothing in the exchange has reversed that. The work answers a first-order question about who gains and loses when technology and trade change labour demand. It combines a conceptual account (skill demand and supply, the race between education and technology, tasks) with transparent designs, such as local labour-market exposure to import competition, that others can re-examine. A decade or more of replication, extension and critique has refined magnitudes and persistence without overturning the qualitative findings. That is the maturity test I apply to every candidate. It is also the kind of cross-disciplinary contribution that moves from theory to measurement to policy. On the chair's scope question, I would write the citation around labour demand, wages and regional employment and not around the task model as theory. That wording rests on the empirical record, which limits the overlap with Acemoglu's recognised task work and with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes, and it also covers Katz's strand. Katz's citable contribution is the long-run evidence on the demand for and supply of skills and the education-technology race. It is a separate body of evidence from the import-competition papers and from his role on B028, and it is what lets the citation say technology as well as trade. I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee prefers a trade-adjustment citation. That would honour the cleanest joint attribution for the China-shock papers, but it would be a narrower prize and the citation should say so, for example: for showing how import competition reshapes local labour markets. I would also regard an Autor-Hanson award as defensible but the weakest of the three versions, because it leaves the skills-and-technology evidence uncredited.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still the cost of the three-name cap. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded, and the task framework has contributors outside the credited names, including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. Whether the technology and trade strands are one achievement or two is a judgment call, and a joint citation can read as two prizes combined, with Autor as the link. The size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects remain debated, so the trade half of the citation rests on the part of the evidence that is most contested. Those effects are also local, and moving from them to aggregate welfare claims takes extra structure. The Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024) prizes reduce the marginal claim somewhat, though I think the questions they addressed are different. If the committee judges that no single citation does justice to both strands, I would prefer a clean originator award such as B006 to a diffuse B027.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file now names Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that the citation should match the credited work, that a trade-shock-only trio would credit half of the achievement, and that the Acemoglu overlap should be handled through wording. He also treats the nine-of-eleven overlap in laureate sets as coincidence, not merit.
responses.response: I agree with the wording argument, and I want to be explicit that I also treat the overlap in our sets as a reason to test the attribution case, not as evidence for it. You answered my opening B018 position, and I should say it has moved. Your point that time-dependent pricing is not uniformly supported by micro price-setting evidence is a fair reason to doubt that a New Keynesian award can be written cleanly. I have therefore dropped B018 from my alternatives. Where I would press you is on the Acemoglu overlap. Wording around labour demand, wages and local labour markets handles it, but the committee should also be able to state in one sentence what is separately new in the Autor-Katz skills evidence and the Autor-Hanson trade evidence. I think it can, and I would ask supporters of the joint citation to write that sentence out loud.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) prefers B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He regards the collateral-amplification mechanism as foundational, cleanly attributed and nearly thirty years old. He keeps Gertler out because of the 2022 overlap, and he rates B027 very strong scientifically but split across two strands whose credit differs.
responses.response: I agree that B006 has the cleanest attribution on the list and that a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore award is better than my own opening three-name set with Gertler. On the chair's question, I do not think the thinner direct identification is disqualifying. I treat it as a reason to rank it below B027, not out of contention, which is why B006 is now my first alternative. My remaining question is the one Teorell put to you: what sentence separates the dynamic asset-price amplification mechanism from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises? Stromberg gives a plausible answer, but a citation needs to state it. Your concern about the two B027 strands is the one I take most seriously. I think it is a question of citation scope and not of merit, and I would support B006 over a B027 citation that cannot be worded as one achievement.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Autor, Katz and Hanson. He says that if the committee decides the citation should concern trade exposure alone, he would support Friberg's Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio. He would word the citation around the empirical demonstration of labour-market effects, not the task model as theory.
responses.response: That is the position I hold too, and I think it is the right way to frame the choice. It is a choice about citation scope, not about who is more meritorious. I disagree on one thing only. I would not concede that Dorn's claim on the trade papers is stronger than Hanson's. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are joint originators, and the case for Hanson is that he anchors the trade-shock evidence across the broader program. The committee would be dropping one of three originators either way, and I would say so openly. If a narrow citation were chosen, I would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson. I take your caution about not treating support counts as merit seriously, and my own change from B018 rested on attribution, not on how others ranked.

responses.point: Stromberg prefers B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that the mechanism is dynamic and works through asset prices, not bank runs, and so is distinct from the 2022 prize. He says Gertler's omission should be explained and that his appearance on B018 should not decide either ballot. He ranks B027 a close second.
responses.response: On Gertler I agree with you and with the point in the chair's summary. A name that appears on two ballots should be judged on the merits of the contribution under each. For B006 the originator claim stands without him, and adding him would blur the citation and import the accelerator overlap that Hassler and Krusell raise. I would explain his omission as a matter of scope and not as a verdict on his work. I find your distinctness argument credible, and it is why B006 is my first alternative. Your own file says B027 is a close second, so we may differ less than the first-place counts suggest. The remaining difference is how much weight to give broad, directly tested empirical confirmation against a clean theoretical attribution, and I put somewhat more weight on the former.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the technology and trade strands as one achievement or two, and so whether the right third name is Katz or Dorn. I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson under a trade-adjustment citation.
How much the 2021, 2023 and 2024 labour, education and technology prizes, and Acemoglu's task work in particular, reduce the marginal claim, and whether wording alone can handle the overlap.
How robust the size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects are, and whether they can anchor half of a citation.
Whether B006 can be separated cleanly from the 2022 prize and the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator lineage, and whether its mainly theoretical status should rank it below B027.
Whether a clean B018 citation exists. I have not found a three-name solution and have dropped it from my alternatives, but the influence of the framework is not in doubt.
My assessments rely on my own reading of the supplied files and my background in microeconomic theory and market design. I have not independently verified any claim.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn (B027), Kiyotaki or Moore (B006), or Helpman or Melitz (B012) is apparent from my profile. My listed co-authors (Svensson, Ehlers, Erlanson, Martinello, Teytelboym, Trapp, Biro and others) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I am an affiliated professor at SSE alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Stromberg, and I co-authored COVID policy work with SSE economists. These are institutional ties to colleagues, not to candidates, and they are disclosed but not adjudicated. My field is microeconomic theory and market design, and my 2020 presentation speech praised cross-disciplinary work that brought theory to practice. That may bias me toward applied, cross-disciplinary contributions such as B027, and I disclose it as a perspective, not a connection. My opening first place, B018, was a macro candidate outside my field, and I have moved off it.
